en: The Scripture Spoken by the Buddha on the Samādhi of Self-Vow, Chapter Four: The Sole Realization, excerpted from the *Bhikṣu-viśuddha-caryā*.
Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the realm of Magadha, staying at a great grove in the hermitage of a brahmin.

Amidst the trees was the Jinglu Vihāra, and the site where he dwelt was named Xianyang Duzheng (Manifesting and Solely Realizing). At the moment he first attained Buddhahood, his radiance was exceedingly brilliant, and a natural rain of jewels fell upon his lotus throne. He was accompanied by a great assembly of thirty-two thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who possessed the dhāraṇīs of mental mastery and fully controlled their faculties, who were sovereign over the three periods of time with unimpeded supernatural powers, and who—like great dragons—had accomplished what was to be done and were perfected in noble wisdom, having thoroughly understood the origins of sentient beings; such as the worthy Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others.

The Bodhisattvas were innumerable, all possessing inconceivable and universal mastery of expedient means; they roamed through the treasuries of all Buddhas and transcended the practices of all Māras. Equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, they propagated the six perfections and great compassion across countless lands, delivering sentient beings according to the times so that they might attain peace. Having distanced themselves from worldly fame and teachings, such eminent leaders as Avalokiteśvara and Maitreya were among them.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata entered the samādhi of divine stillness and spiritual realization, universally reaching all Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Before the Buddha’s seat, a lotus throne suddenly and spontaneously surged forth from the earth; its fragrance was pure and its radiance permeated the ten directions. This flower had a thousand petals, and upon each petal stood a transformed bodhisattva, attending in solemn order while dwelling mysteriously in the void. Each, from their respective positions, prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, circumambulated seven times to the right, and then stood respectfully before him. Together they raised their voices in a great sound, praising what had never before occurred: "So it is, World-Honored One!"

We ourselves have seen in our own original lands a transformed, numinous, and auspicious tree; when this tree first sprouted, its light illuminated Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. From the tree issued a great sound, pure and clear, mournful yet elegant, compassionate and harmonious, flowing deeply into the hearts of all beings. Those who heard it leaped for joy, becoming fully endowed with equanimity, giving rise to the practices of the Mahāyāna and the six pāramitās, and completely perfecting the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all Buddha-works.
At that time, each of the Tathāgatas in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges dispatched a bodhisattva to proclaim the Way and illuminate the Mahāyāna, addressing those bodhisattvas, saying:

"From this buddha-field, you must cross over as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges until you reach a buddha-field named Sahā—in the language of Han, 'Endurance World. There, the Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he performs the work of a Buddha through the Dharma and Vinaya, supernormal powers, and verbal instruction."
Each Tathāgata held a thousand-petaled lotus flower in his hand, presented it to the Bodhisattva, and addressed him, saying:

"Bear our names and pay infinite homage. We rejoice that you, O Righteous Man, have accomplished your merit and fulfilled your vow; your realization of the Way is complete. You have descended into this world of five turbidities to shoulder the heavy responsibility for the sake of all beings. Leaping over the ranks, you stand before Maitreya; with great compassion and the six perfections, you universally rescue all living beings. Your daily life is light and well-being, and your teaching of the Way surpasses the ordinary. We now present these flowers as a Dharma-offering, wishing that all may assemble together at the site of enlightenment."

Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, those bodhisattvas suddenly vanished from their respective lands and entered the profound stillness of *samādhi* and the contemplative state of *vipaśyanā*. In an instant, they all arrived in the Sahā world. Each left his seat and stood upright with dignified decorum, paying homage to the sacred transformation by prostrating himself on the ground. He then circumambulated the Buddha seven times before withdrawing to his original position. With their supernormal powers abiding in the profound and their deportment solemn and majestic, their dharma robes perfectly aligned, they raised their voices in unison and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Our World-Honored One, the Tathāgatas of our native lands send immeasurable greetings. We rejoice that you have fulfilled your vows and perfected your resolve, fully embodying the essence of the Way. You have manifested your spirit within the five turbidities to shoulder the heavy responsibility for the multitude; you have transcended the ranks of others to stand before Maitreya. Through the great compassion of the six perfections, you universally save all living beings; your health and well-being are as excellent as ever, and your teachings surpass the ordinary."
"I now present these flowers as a Dharma-offering, wishing that all beings may universally assemble at this site of enlightenment.
The Buddha said,
"Virtuous One!"

I joyfully receive the teachings of wisdom from those Tathāgatas without weariness; my samādhi is fully developed, and the dharmakāya is empty, pure, and endowed with vast, brilliant wisdom. This and that are of one essence, and I reverently sing of what I have heard, filled with immeasurable light and joy.

At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni accepted these flowers with his own hand and smiled joyfully. Light issued from his mouth, universally illuminating the infinite Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. He then scattered these flowers equally upon those infinite Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and likewise caused his radiance to penetrate and pervade those worlds throughout their entirety. Every sentient being who encountered the Buddha’s compassionate light attained the vision of wisdom and the realization of past lives. They illuminated one another in succession, shining even down into the hells; whether in the three evil realms, the eight difficulties, the heavens, or among humans, all were graced by the compassionate light and attained liberation. Hundreds of thousands of beings became of one mind, universally resolving to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of enlightenment.
The light immediately returned, circled his body three times, and vanished into the crown of his head.

At that moment, all the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, could see one another clearly; through the majestic spiritual power of these Buddhas, all sentient beings were enabled to behold them. Once the manifestation of transformations was complete, everything became vast and empty, returning to its ordinary state.
Then, among those in the assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Xianru (Wise Scholar) who, before the Buddha, praised him with these verses:
"How wondrous is the Great Sage’s transformation! He takes pity on all classes of living beings.
From incalculable kalpas past, He has accumulated meritorious deeds."
Each and every meritorious deed, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, constitutes a single mark through a hundred blessings;
I pray to pay homage to the Honored One of the three periods.
How wondrous is the Great Sage’s transformation—his compassion and wisdom are boundless!
The Daoists are pure and noble; the Buddhist Master is the God among Gods.
His great wisdom is supreme and unsurpassed; his Dharma-boat delivers all living beings.
His holy insight is pure and immeasurable; I vow to pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
How wondrous is the transformation of the Great Sage! The compassionate light moistens beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
Ignorance and darkness are entirely dispelled, And the turbid confusion of delusion is turned into clarity.
His gracious benefits accord with the needs of the times, And his skillful means embrace all living beings.
"The Dharma-bridge delivers all beings; I vow to pay homage to the Honored One of the Three Realms.
Thereupon, the Holy Teacher said to the worthy scholar:
"The smile of the Buddhas has three causes and conditions."

What are these three? The wisdom of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is profound, far-reaching, subtle, and wondrous; it illuminates the three periods of time and penetrates the origin of sentient beings. The inclinations of those following the three vehicles each possess their own fundamental practices, faculties, and convictions. There are some bodhisattvas whose resolve lies in great vows; they don the armor of great virtue for the heavy responsibility of the masses, severing the paths [of delusion] to serve as bridges for the world. They are single-mindedly devoted to the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) without abandoning anything; abiding in the Way, they gradually manifest courageous and vigorous progress. Their practice of giving is signless (*animitta*), and they maintain the precepts, patience, and protective conduct; their meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is undisturbed, and their wisdom (*prajñā*) is clear and bright as they advance toward non-retrogression.
O worthy scholars! With the Buddha-eye, I see that each and every one of these has received their prediction of enlightenment;
it is not only a single Buddha who grants them this prediction, but all the Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions grant them their predictions as well.

This is one causal condition. "Furthermore, O worthy scholar! If there is a bodhisattva who is directed toward the stage of *avaivartika*, who has accumulated the roots of virtue and is fully endowed with noble wisdom; who makes offerings to immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, receiving a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) from each one, with each prediction clarifying the next; who purifies Buddha-lands and equally moistens sentient beings through a universal single practice; who summons the Buddhas, sages, and great benevolent ones to serve as a great Dharma-ship across the four swift currents; who exhausts the sea of the six desires and dries up the twelve gates; who enters the five paths and purifies the five eyes; who concentrates his spirit in profound stillness while dwelling in the Tuṣita palace; who gathers all bodhisattvas, realized ones, and upright men; and who purifies the conduct within the three realms to expound the wheel of non-retrogression."

The Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions all join in praising such bodhisattvas before the fourfold assembly, extolling their virtues and declaring that they shall soon descend as spirits to become Buddhas, whereby all sentient beings throughout the ten directions will universally attain liberation.
These are the two causes and conditions.
Furthermore, O worthy scholar!

If there is a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita palace who, having completed his lifespan in that heaven, is about to descend and manifest his incarnation, he then enters the Samādhi of Ultimate Universal Manifestation.

The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens surveyed the entire trichiliocosm, observing that the kingdoms and cities were vast and the sentient beings gentle and harmonious; among the kṣatriyas, brahmins, elders, and householders within the billions of cities and towns, there was one who possessed the Way and virtue, pure, sincere, benevolent, kind, and compassionate—a Wheel-Turning Sage King dwelling in India. The gods deliberated on his descent into a spirit-conception, with the celestial hosts attending him; he appeared dwelling in the palace amidst maidservants and guards, appearing to study worldly affairs and contemplate the four marks of impermanence.

Encouraged by the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven to renounce the world, he entered the mountains to refine his practice, sitting beneath a peepal tree. He shaved his hair and took a vow to assume the form of a bhikṣu; he cultivated the teachings of the former Buddhas, taking the Dharma as his teacher and the Śuddhāvāsa devas as his witnesses.
In a single night, he attained the threefold transcendence and subdued the hosts of Māra’s officials, fully accomplishing the Buddha-work.

Auspicious and miraculous trees appeared throughout as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges; in each of those lands, every Tathāgata, amidst the eight classes of beings, praised the merits of the Bodhisattva and his seat-tree.
In this manner, each [Buddha] dispatched bodhisattvas from their respective lands to present flowers, pay homage, and extol the Mahāyāna.

O worthy ones! All the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions are fully aware of this; they rejoice in the virtuous celebration as sentient beings gather universally at the site of enlightenment.
These are the three causes and conditions.

"Those bodhisattvas who have come here are all those with whom the Tathāgata shared past causal conditions; because they have heard this teaching of the Dharma, they shall all attain the state of non-arising. Whether they are headed toward the stage of the Youthful (Kumārabhūta), or toward the stage of Birth (Janman), or toward the stage of Non-retrogression (Avaivartika), the Tathāgata has bestowed upon each of them a clear and complete prediction of their future enlightenment."
"Know this, O Noble One! The Buddha does not smile without cause.

When these words were spoken, seventy billion nayutas of bodhisattvas attained the stage of the Youthful (kumārabhūta); sixty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas attained the stage of being born [into the family] (gotrabhū); thirty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas attained the state of non-retrogression (avaivartika); one hundred thousand bhikṣus attained arhatship; nine billion nayutas of people attained entry into the tracks of the Path; and all the devas of the three realms universally obtained the light of the Dharma.
Thereupon, the Holy Teacher composed this verse:
“The Dharma-realm is entirely empty; The form-body is pure and true.
Dhāraṇī is the perfection of liberation; Samādhi has no cause.”
"The Buddha-realm is not empty, yet the purity of wisdom is not existent.
Out of compassion for the world, he manifests a smile; O Noble One, you should quickly accept it.

Thereupon, among those in the assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Vidyutprabhābhadra. He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and stepped forward to address the Holy Master:
"I wish to ask a question; may the Holy Teacher, with his immeasurable wisdom, illuminate and explain that which I have not yet heard.
The World-Honored One said, "Excellent!"
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall now fully expound the essential points for you.
The Bodhisattva Mingjian Guangxian said, "What is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva leaving the household life, fulfilling the realization of the Way, and attaining *samyaksambodhi*?"
Thereupon the Holy Teacher said: "Virtuous one!
Listen well and fix your attention; contemplate thoroughly its essential points."
For all Buddhas to leave the household life, there must first be an initial resolve; they sit upright in quietude, contemplating the profound and subtle mysteries.

When one focuses single-mindedly on mindfulness of the Way, there is inevitably a response. In response to this resonance, the devas of the Pure Abodes and the Sovereign Brahma King commanded Śakra to manifest the four signs of impermanence—the forms of old age, sickness, death, and suffering. Through these, he preached the realization of liberation from the hardships of desire and suffering.

Contemplating the purity of the Way, he resolved to dwell in the mountains and marshes to refine his essence and practice dhyāna; this intention was then firmly established. From the Four Heavenly Kings downward, they provided him with service as required.

He proceeded to the Pippala tree, recollecting the methods of renunciation practiced by former Buddhas, taking the Dharma as his teacher and the devas and Brahmās as witnesses. His faculty of faith was solidified within, and he cultivated the six pāramitās from past habituation, as well as the four immeasurables, the four debts of gratitude, and the four dhyānas. He exercised the five supernormal powers and skillful means according to the occasion, and fully realized the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment for the sake of Buddha-work. Since first conceiving his resolve, he had never abandoned anything, until suddenly he attained self-awakening.
Śakra then descended and handed him a razor. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva held his hair with his left hand and took the razor in his right, thinking to himself:

"I shall reap the habitual defilements of suffering and plant the roots of non-attachment; I shall sever the flow of non-retrogression and penetrate the source of Nirvana. From the moment I first conceived this intention, I have always maintained the state of leaving home; my firm resolve is never weary, my profound non-retrogressive faith is fully realized, and my mental intent is clear and distinct."
Before the blade had even reached his hair, it fell away of its own accord, and the *uṣṇīṣa* became naturally manifest.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"When previous Buddhas left the home life and shaved their hair, there must have been the dharma-garment of the *kāṣāya*."

Just as he was examining his mind and giving rise to this thought, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven took a *karpāsa* robe that had appeared spontaneously in the heavens of the Form Realm and offered it to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"I pray that the Righteous One will accept this Dharma-robe."

The Bodhisattva immediately accepted them and donned them upon his body; they fit him perfectly, and his majestic demeanor became solemn and dignified. Thereupon, throughout the infinite worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all the Buddhas perceived one another through their mutual penetration and each sent a *kāṣāya* robe to bestow upon the Bodhisattva, whom the Bodhisattva then accepted from all those Buddhas.

The majestic spiritual powers of all those Buddhas manifested universally, causing the robes sent by each Buddha to merge into a single garment, named the *Sāṃkakṣikā* (or *Saṃghāṭī*) of the Buddha’s Head.
This robe is now in the Brahma Heaven.
For this reason, I sat upright for six years to exhaust my past karmic conditions; after those six years, at the end of the night, the realization of the precepts finally manifested.
What is meant by the "realization of the precepts"?
Their aspiration lies in the seclusion of mountains and marshes where they receive the Dharma; their spirits are true and their conduct far-reaching as they uphold the precepts and practice the Way.
They do not begrudge their lives nor discard their bodies; they regard all things with equanimity and seek no profit or sustenance.

Guarding emptiness and practicing stillness, they constantly contemplate pure dharmas; they practice the four pure immeasurables—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—and proclaim the four debts of gratitude through generous giving.
Loved by people, benefiting others with impartial benefit, endowed with unsurpassed compassion, clearly explaining the four dhyānas as being without flaw or defilement,
without clever conceptualization, distancing oneself from eye-forms, relinquishing ear-sounds, ceasing nose-odors, severing the flavors of the tongue,
ending external tactile pleasures, stilling mental intentions, extinguishing the six desires, abandoning former habits, and bringing form to rest— form.
Sounds and fragrances cease; tastes and the relish for tastes cease; the thought of pleasure ceases. With the cessation of such thoughts, pure form arises.
One cuts off the sounds of the ear, stills the faculty of the nose, uproots the power of the mouth, and rests in the meditative concentration of the awakening mind.
Whether form or non-form, there is no non-form; there is no extinction of form, nor is there form within form. One relinquishes the great elements and abandons fundamental habits.

Sound is not sound; there is no non-sound; it is neither sound nor non-sound. Abandoning that reception, this arising ceases; without conditions or opposition, one returns to the fundamental severance.
Fragrance is not fragrance; there is no non-fragrance; it is neither fragrance nor non-fragrance. The spirit is empty and pure; with a pure spirit, one possesses the supernormal powers.
Taste is not taste; there is no non-taste; it is neither taste nor non-taste. Tranquility weakens [the defilements], while the faculties and powers grow strong.
Pleasure is not pleasure; it is not non-pleasure; it does not delight in pleasure. The four great elements are pure; they abide in purity from the very beginning.

As for mind, thought, and consciousness, they take the seven dharmas as their objects; these seven dharmas are pure, and purity is their destination. The mind is no-mind, yet it is not a mind that is not a mind; the intellect is no-intellect, yet it is not an intellect that is not an intellect; consciousness is no-consciousness, yet it is not a non-consciousness, nor is it a consciousness that is consciousness; it is not mental consciousness. These combined become one.
By knowing the one, one eliminates the one; there is no movement within the one. The ground of emptiness is fundamental, and the direction toward purity is fundamental.

One abandons fame and reputation, relinquishes the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and is without seed-nature (*gotra*). One does not follow the crowd, stays far from laws and punishments, and is without self (*ātman*) or person (*pudgala*).
One abandons the seeking for life and has no perception of the three realms (*tridhātu*). There is no...
Consciousness is without self, without a person, without a life-principle, without a soul; it is without name, without lineage, without transformation, and without number;
it is without action, coming from nowhere and going nowhere; it is without arising and without ceasing;
it is without body and without transgression, without mouth and without speech, without mind and without thought, and without worldly affairs.
Without conceptualization, without objective conditions, without abiding, and neither possessing precepts nor maintaining them;
without thoughts of accomplishment and without thoughts of destruction— this is called the prohibitive precepts, the pure precepts of inner and outer,
and the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts.
Free from blemish and without attachment to precepts, without anger or resentment, stable and pure, he proceeds upon the path to transcendence.

When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva first sat beneath the tree, he initially realized the purity of the precepts; he abandoned the root of suffering that is desire, relinquished distracted thoughts, and was without arising thoughts, unshakable thoughts, subtle thoughts, thoughts of self, thoughts of others, or thoughts of the middle.

There is no perception of self or other, no perception of internal or external, no perception of the Path, no perception of the mundane, no perception of cessation, no perception of the non-existence of cessation, no perception of the non-existence of the non-existence of non-existence, and no perception of the non-existence of the non-existence of non-existence; there is no perception of exhaustion or non-exhaustion.
"Thus it is, O Noble One!
As the Bodhisattva sat beneath the tree, he established the foundation of pure faith through the eighteen hundred precepts.

When this number was completed, the Vajra-seat suddenly split from the earth and emerged; the sixth realm of Māra trembled violently, and the devas of the three worlds were unsettled in their positions. They all descended together to the Pippala tree to offer service and attend to him as was fitting."
Suddenly, a great sound arose throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and within that great sound it was said:
"The Bodhisattva sitting beneath the tree shall this night attain realization.
All sentient beings heard it and saw it.
Thus it is, O noble son!

This is how a bodhisattva fulfills the precepts and realizes *samyaksambodhi*, becoming fully endowed with the three types of knowledge, the six supernormal powers, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities, the ten powers, the supernatural faculties, and the four fearlessnesses.

The three-thousandfold world system shook in six ways; his merit subdued Māra, and his radiance shone universally throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Sentient beings, receiving this compassionate light, simultaneously attained peace and universally resolved to seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, eight hundred bhikṣus attained arhatship; thirty thousand devas and humans all attained the Dharma-eye; three thousand lay practitioners (upāsakas) attained the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin); and the worthy scholars and virtuous gentlemen all returned to the end of their births. The entire assembly universally resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Thereupon the Holy Master addressed the worthy Confucian, saying: "In the past, at one time I was traveling through the kingdom of Kuśinagara.

At that moment, a faction of celestial Māras suddenly arrived with their followers and entered the great assembly. Wearing strange garments, they mingled with the multitude, engaging in disputes and litigation, and mutually slandering one another with discordant clamor. The bhikṣus, being unacquainted with the essence of the Way, became filled with resentment and agitation; each broke away from the group and fled in different directions, while only the Arhats and True Persons retired to the mountains and forests."
At that time, O worthy scholar!

When the three months of summer had passed and the end of the year had arrived, on the fourteenth day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, at night when the morning star appeared, he gave instructions only to Ānanda to strike the *gandī* and spread the grass mats, intending to perform the *pravāraṇā* together with Ānanda alone.
At that time, a devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven addressed the Buddha from mid-air:
"World-Honored One!
Now that the assembly of bhikṣus has dispersed in various directions, why does the Buddha observe the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) all alone?"
The Buddha told the devaputra:

"In the past, when I left the household life, you were my witness; when I went to the Pāṭali tree, you again were my witness; now that I have completed the rains retreat, you again are my witness. Throughout Jambudvīpa and the surrounding three thousandfold world system, in immeasurable worlds, the Tathāgata has attained *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge)."
From the moment of attaining Buddhahood until entering *nirvāṇa*, you have served as a witness, fully endowed with the three bodies of proof.
You should know, O Son of Heaven!

Even the *tathāgata*s, with their path-wisdom and supernormal powers, must still rely on witnesses for their solitary progress through the triple world; how much more so for all ordinary beings who seek the Way—could they do without a teacher?
He further addressed the Śuddhāvāsa deities:

"In the final age, many people will set their wills upon purity; their aspiration for the Way will be steadfast and clear, and they will take no pleasure in worldly things, choosing instead to dwell in seclusion within mountain forests. They will truly possess a firm resolve to leave the household life."

If there is no teacher or elder to follow as a model, one should follow the method of renunciation practiced by Mahākāśyapa: taking the distancing from desire and its abandonment as proof; taking the distancing from the mundane and its abandonment as proof; taking the distancing from fame and renown and their abandonment as proof; taking the distancing from physical form and the forgetting of form as proof; and taking the distancing from internal and external seeking and the abandonment of seeking as proof.

"O Devaputra! By means of these five proofs, Mahākāśyapa shaved off his beard and hair and donned the kāṣāya. He took the naturally pure Dharma as his teacher and moved the Buddhas of the ten directions to seek his compassion and hear his confession. Reflecting upon the Buddha’s way of leaving the household life, he invoked the Pure Abodes as witnesses; with these three clear proofs, he became a bhikṣu. He practiced the twelve dhūtas exclusively, remaining firm in each one without giving rise to thoughts of seeking personal realization."
At that time, Kāśyapa attained the five supernormal powers beneath the tree; finally, upon seeing the Buddha, he became fully endowed with the six supernormal powers.

Thus it is, O Devaputra! Monks in the final age should contemplate this Dharma well. They must not be arrogant, seeking fame by disparaging the assembly in hopes of offerings. Nor should they claim to possess this Dharma while turning their backs on the community and refusing to take a teacher. Regarding this Dharma and the teachers, one should realize that there are no monks at all who can serve as teachers for this practice. If there is a Saṃgha, one should seek the Saṃgha as witnesses. For the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha—these Three Jewels—are equal to the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Tathāgata praised the assembly of monks who uphold the Vinaya as being foremost. You should know this, O Devaputra!
"Within the community of bhikṣus, there will surely be those of the three vehicles.
When these words were spoken, the devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven and the assemblies of the eight classes of beings rejoiced upon hearing the sūtra; they paid homage and departed.
The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Self-Vow Spoken by the Buddha
